To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the majority (98%) of community isolates of urinary tract bacteria were sensitive to the fluoroquinolones, and that the majority of these isolates were also sensitive to co-amoxiclv and trimethoprim.
98.9%, 98.9 and 95.7 of isolates were sensitive to norfioxacin, ciprofloxaxin and co-amoxiclav respectively.

the sensitivity of bacteria isolated from community patients with urinary tract infections to commonly used antimicrobials varies considerably between laboratories, that there are differences in sensitivity between different centres in Britain and that the use of standard breakpoint sensitivity values may result in overestimation of the sensitivity of urinary isolates to some antimicrobials.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods of analysis and the application of new techniques to the analysis of data.
the identification of the bacterial species most frequently isolated from patients with urinary tract infection, and with the sensitivity of these species to a range of oral antimicrobial agents.
the identification of the bacteria responsible for community-acquired urinary infection, and the sensitivity of these bacteria to the most widely prescribed antibiotics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the quinolone antibiotics are the most effective antimicrobials for the empirical treatment of community-acquired urinary infection in Britain.

, in this survey, 98.8% of urinary isolates were sensitive to co-amoxiclov, 98.7% to norfloxaxin and ciprofloxaxin, 97.3% to cephlexin, 96.9% to trimethoprin, 94.7% to nitrofunantoin, and 91.7% to cefradine.
all of the drugs tested are of value in urinary tract infection, although there are differences in the sensitivities of the organisms isolated from different parts of the country.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the sensitivity of community isolates to the quinone antimicrobials and to the beta-lactams was generally good, although the sensitivity of the latter to the cephalosprins was less than that of the quinolone.

98.9, 98.8 and 98.7% of isolates would have been sensitive to norfioxacin, ciprofloxaxin and co-amoxiclav respectively if these agents had been used as the first choice in the management of urinary tract infection in these patients.
the quinolone antibiotics are highly active against community urinary isolates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need to standardize the breakpoints used in different laboratories, as well as the methods used to determine sensitivities.
the use of standardised susceptibility breakpoints for the interpretation of antibiotic susceptibility testing results is critical.

the use of standard breakpoints for the interpretation of antimicrobial susceptibility testing results may result in misleading conclusions about the usefulness of antimicrobial agents for the treatment of urinary tract infection.
